sentences: Broken slabs of ice are stacked layer upon layer, rising toward the sky.
This is The Sea of Ice, painted by the German Romantic artist Caspar David Friedrich.
There is no person in sight, no path to follow, and nowhere for the eye to rest comfortably.
There is no warm light either.
Cold blues, greys and pale greens fill the whole canvas.
The first impression is of a silence so complete that it almost takes your breath away.
Friedrich wants us to feel how small we are in front of nature.
Friedrich worked in Dresden and spent his life painting the smallness of human beings before nature.
Many people know him from his picture of a wanderer gazing over a sea of fog.
In The Sea of Ice, he goes one step further and removes the human figure altogether.
In the winter of 1820 to 1821, he made oil studies of ice floes drifting on the Elbe near Dresden.
Those careful observations of real ice seem to have found their way into this painting.
The edges, the cracks and the thickness of each slab feel studied from life.
It is often suggested that reports of a British expedition searching for an Arctic sea route also inspired him.
That link, however, has never been confirmed.
What is certain is that the polar world was a source of fascination and fear for Europeans at the time.
Now look at the centre of the canvas.
Flat plates of ice lean and overlap until they form a sharp peak.
It looks almost built, like a tower or a tomb raised by some unseen hand.
The jagged diagonal lines give the still scene a sense of violent force.
Now look beside the pile.
A ship lies half buried among the slabs, crushed and swallowed by the ice.
Next to the great frozen mass it looks pitifully small, as if it will soon vanish completely.
It is the only trace of human ambition in the picture.
Toward the horizon, the ice field stretches on and on.
The sky is clear, but cold.
There is no harbour, no shore and no way out.
Friedrich turns a landscape into a feeling of the sublime, that mixture of awe and dread before something far larger than ourselves.
The painting was first shown at the Prague Academy in 1824.
Visitors and critics were puzzled by its unusual subject and composition.
A painting with no figures and no story, only ice and a wreck, was very hard to accept at the time.
It was still unsold when Friedrich died in 1840.
Only later did its daring become clear, and today it is counted among his masterpieces.
It hangs in the Hamburger Kunsthalle, where it remains one of the most memorable pictures of winter in European art.
Step back and take in the whole scene again.
Then ask yourself honestly how it makes you feel.
Does the ice frighten you, or does its vast silence strangely calm your mind?
